name: Roots
kicker: Underground plant organs · Anchor the plant and soak up water and minerals
dates: Grow from the radicle of a sprouting seed
briefing: Roots anchor a plant and drink for it, soaking up water and minerals through countless microscopic root hairs. Some store food, which is why we eat carrots, beets, and sweet potatoes, though an ordinary potato is actually a stem. Others grow in surprising directions: mangroves send “breathing” roots up out of the mud, and banyan trees drop roots from their branches that thicken into pillars.
answerHtml: Roots (accept root, root system, or taproot; prompt on root hairs, root cap, or radicle; do not accept “stems” or “rhizomes”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A waxy band of suberin [“SOO-ber-in”] called the Casparian [“kas-PAIR-ee-un”] strip runs through the cell walls of the endodermis in these organs, forcing water and minerals to pass through living cell membranes before reaching the xylem. Just inside that endodermis lies the pericycle, where new side branches of these organs begin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that absorb water and minerals from the soil and anchor plants in the ground.

tossups.p: Starch-filled grains called statoliths settle to the bottom of cells near the tips of these organs, telling them which way is down. That signal lets these organs bend toward gravity, a response called positive gravitropism.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that grow down into the soil to soak up water, protected at their tips by a cap of cells.

tossups.p: A cluster of slowly dividing cells called the quiescent [“kwee-ESS-ent”] center sits near the tip of these organs. Behind each tip, these organs have a zone of cell division, a zone of elongation where cells stretch, and a zone of maturation where tiny hairs sprout.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that absorb water and minerals from the soil and hold plants in place.

tossups.p: Water entering these organs can travel through cell walls, called the apoplast, or through the cytoplasm of cells joined by tiny channels, called the symplast. Pressure built up in these organs at night can push droplets of water out of the leaf edges of grasses and strawberries, a process called guttation [“guh-TAY-shun”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs covered in tiny hairs that absorb water and minerals from the soil.

tossups.p: Orchids that grow high on tree branches have aerial versions of these organs wrapped in a spongy, silvery layer called velamen [“vuh-LAY-men”] that soaks up rainwater. Banyan trees drop aerial ones from their branches that thicken into pillars looking like extra trunks.
tossups.r: Most of these organs grow underground. For 10 points, name these plant organs that anchor a plant and absorb water from the soil.

tossups.p: Black mangroves grow pneumatophores [“noo-MAT-uh-forz”], special versions of these organs that poke up out of the mud like snorkels to take in air. Red mangroves and corn plants are braced by “prop” versions of these organs that grow down from their stems.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs, which usually grow underground to absorb water and minerals.

tossups.p: Most plants trade sugar to fungi that grow around or into these organs, forming partnerships called mycorrhizae [“my-koh-RYE-zee”] that help them collect water and phosphorus. Legumes like peas also house nitrogen-fixing _Rhizobium_ [“rye-ZOH-bee-um”] bacteria in nodules on these organs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that anchor a plant and absorb water from the soil, often through tiny hairs.

tossups.p: Black walnut trees release juglone [“JOO-glone”], a chemical that harms nearby tomato plants, partly from these organs, an example of allelopathy [“uh-lee-LOP-uh-thee”]. The tips of these organs make much of a plant’s supply of cytokinins [“sye-toh-KYE-ninz”], hormones that trigger cell division.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that absorb water and minerals, often through tiny hairs.

tossups.p: Dodder, a parasitic vine, loses these organs once it latches onto a host and then feeds through suckers called haustoria [“haw-STOR-ee-uh”]. Mosses have no true versions of these organs and instead cling to surfaces with thread-like rhizoids [“RYE-zoydz”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs, which in most plants anchor them in the soil and absorb water.

tossups.p: Lilies and many other bulb-forming plants grow contractile versions of these organs, which shrink lengthwise to tug the bulb deeper into the soil. Sweet potatoes and cassava are swollen versions of these organs, but ordinary potatoes are not; potatoes are underground stems called tubers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs, including edible carrots and beets, that absorb water from the soil.

tossups.p: The radicle [“RAD-ih-kul”], the first part of a sprouting seed to break out of the seed coat, develops into the first of these organs. As one of these organs pushes through soil, the protective cap at its tip is constantly worn away and replaced.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that anchor a plant and absorb water through tiny hairs.

tossups.p: Versions of these organs that grow from a stem or leaf, instead of from the radicle of a seed, are called adventitious [“ad-ven-TISH-us”]. Gardeners dip stem cuttings in powders containing auxins, such as IBA, to make new ones of these organs sprout.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that grow underground and absorb water and minerals from the soil.

tossups.p: In buttercups and other eudicots, the xylem at the center of these organs forms an X or star shape when cut crosswise, while in corn and other monocots the xylem and phloem form a ring around a soft central pith.
tossups.r: Grasses usually have a fibrous system of these organs instead of one thick main one. For 10 points, name these underground plant organs that absorb water and minerals.

tossups.p: Overwatering can kill a houseplant because soggy soil leaves these organs without the oxygen they need for cellular respiration. Most of these organs lack chlorophyll, so they depend on sugar sent down from the leaves through the phloem.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that take in water and minerals through tiny hairs.

tossups.p: Dandelions are hard to pull up because they have one long, thick main one of these organs, while grasses form a fibrous mat of thin ones that helps hold soil in place and prevent erosion.
tossups.r: Carrots and radishes are swollen versions of these organs. For 10 points, name these plant organs that anchor plants and absorb water.

trap.title: Potatoes are stems!
trap.body: Plenty of underground plant parts are not roots. Potatoes are tubers (swollen underground stems), ginger is a rhizome (another underground stem), and onions are bulbs made of fleshy leaves, while carrots, beets, and sweet potatoes really are roots. Mosses don’t have true roots at all; their rhizoids only look like them.
trap.fix: A potato’s “eyes” are buds growing from nodes, a feature of stems. If the clues mention root hairs, a root cap, a Casparian strip, or absorbing water and minerals, answer roots, not stems or rhizomes.
trap.line: Real answer line: Roots (accept root system or taproot; do not accept “stems,” “tubers,” “rhizomes,” or “rhizoids”)
